articles.content: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in the 1930s go on show at the Pitt Rivers Museum In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions. They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets. Continue reading...

articles.content: Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found. The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991. Continue reading...

articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: New data offers shocking details of military fatalities. But without domestic accountability, only external pressure can end this conflict The toll of Russia’s war on Ukraine is appallingly evident in the devastation of apartment blocks and hospitals, in the suffering of survivors and, above all, in the mourning of the dead, which included an estimated 150,000 soldiers and at least 18,000 civilians. The toll on Russia’s population has been carefully obscured by Moscow. But a fuller picture has emerged from its own statistics after the hacking group Cyber Partisans, linked to the Belarusian opposition, and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow obtained 11m death certificates. Analysis by the Guardian offers disturbing insights into the deaths of almost half a million Russians in Ukraine since Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022. articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: Ministers have recognised that young adults need more support. But children’s social care reform must go deeper The first lifelong guardianship ceremonies , held in Northampton last week with Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, among the guests, are the latest in a series of measures aimed at boosting support for care leavers. While the decision to register a link between a person who has been looked after as a child and another adult such as a former carer or friend does not carry legal obligations, those involved spoke movingly about what it meant for these relationships to be formally recognised. New rules requiring councils to support contact between siblings in the care system are similarly aimed at strengthening networks that could sustain them beyond childhood into adult life. Belatedly, the government is acting on a mound of evidence that children who are taken into local authority care are frequently acutely vulnerable when they come out of it as 18-year-olds. Care leavers are over-represented in prisons and homeless shelters, and among those who are not in education, employment or training. In August, the Department for Education published an analysis of 112 deaths of care leavers aged between 18 and 24 in 2025, which made for devastating reading. articles.content: Two former Treasury officials say the value of competition and disruption has become ‘the blind spot of UK economic policy’ The defenestration of Marcus Bokkerink in the Keir Starmer-Rachel Reeves era is half-forgotten now – but the saga was a big deal in January 2025 and should still matter to those at the top of today’s government. Bokkerink was chair of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) until he was turfed out because, it seemed, he was deemed insufficiently aligned with the Starmer-Reeves idea that regulators should “support growth”. Bokkerink hit back by warning of the dangers of political interference and competition authorities becoming “vulnerable to short-term expediency or vested interests”. Continue reading...

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.content: Stephen Childs responds to a letter that said the US software firm was not the right fit for Britain’s health service Prof Caroline Mitchell is right that US systems designed for an insurance market are rife in the NHS ( Letters, 18 November ). But Palantir’s software isn’t among them – and should not be confused with a range of other systems, some designed as far back as the 1970s for billing and then exported to the NHS over the following decades. Our story is different. Each application built on the federated data platform – which connects information across the NHS – is bespoke to the NHS and to the healthcare trust that uses it. The NHS is a highly complex, loose association of healthcare trusts and commissioners, with data that is rich, but often unstructured and frustratingly disconnected. Continue reading...

articles.author: Julie Ward
articles.content: My friend Alison Walton-Robson, who has died aged 61 of ovarian cancer, was a tireless campaigner for the disability arts movement. Latterly she was the creative director of Headway Arts in Blyth, Northumberland, a pioneering inclusive organisation she co-founded in 1995. Headway offers people from all backgrounds the chance to contribute to the cultural life of their communities and to realise their full creative potential. The company, which became an Arts Council England national portfolio organisation in 2023, pays particular attention to providing opportunities for artists who are neurodivergent or have a learning disability, and has built an impressive portfolio of projects, including international collaborations. Allie was proud to be an Erasmus+ ambassador and contributed a case study to the European Movement’s successful campaign for the UK to rejoin the EU Erasmus+ education and training programme. Continue reading...

articles.author: Polly Toynbee
articles.content: High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1 When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.” They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. articles.content: King’s theatre, Glasgow The offensive stereotypes have been ditched but this glitzy panto starring Elaine C Smith shoehorns in plenty of irrelevant material Staging a traditional Aladdin in 2026 is problematic. All those laundry scenes, acrobatics and faux Chinese names have the unpleasant whiff of orientalism. In that sense, it is good to see this glitzy mainstream panto, scripted by Alan McHugh for Crossroads, ditching all that. If only it had not thrown the genie out with the bath water. Stereotypes aside, Aladdin can still be a gripping coming-of-age story about greed and gullibility, poverty and power. The stakes can be loaded with deceit, jeopardy and cunning. In this version, set in the land of Pantomania, almost none of that survives. Continue reading...

articles.content: Brighton Dome Boasting all their original members, the quartet put on an extraordinarily eclectic and entertaining show, held together by pure ferocity Few punk bands looked destined to make old bones – longevity wasn’t really the point – but you might have got particularly long odds on the Damned lasting any kind of distance. They were “the Bash Street Kids of punk”, in writer Jon Savage’s memorable estimation: “While other groups were carefully considering their moves,” he wrote, “the Damned went out there and pulled faces at the world as if there was no tomorrow.” Even their debut single New Rose implied they knew their time was limited: “I better go,” sang Dave Vanian amid its frantic thunder, “or it’ll be too late.” How wrong can you be? Their peers are long gone or too riven by bad blood to work together, but the Damned are the one major punk band to observe the movement’s 50th anniversary with every surviving original member onstage, something you get the impression even the Damned are faintly startled by. “This is the kind of venue that would have told us to fuck off 50 years ago,” muses guitarist Captain Sensible, as he gazes around the Dome’s stately auditorium. Impressively, a substantial chunk of the audience respond by shouting “fuck off” in unison. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Bayern Reserve, the German champions’ starting lineup resembled a pale facsimile of its usual self. Their current knack-list includes such high-profile names as – deep breath – Harry Kane, Michael Olise, Alphonso Davies, Manuel Neuer, Serge Gnabry, Luis Díaz, Jamal Musiala and Ismael Saibari. And with Díaz and Musiala only fit enough for places on the bench, Konrad Laimer was deployed as a makeshift striker. The veteran right-back is famously as handy as a small pot, but filling Kane’s iconic Skechers proved a task too far for the Austrian. I liked Erling Haaland’s observation that football can simultaneously be “easy and difficult” [yesterday’s Football Daily]. That got me thinking about other things that have conflicting characteristics. Soup can be both sweet and sour. My feelings for my partner often run hot and cold. And my daily tea-timely newsletter can be mildly funny and mildly unfunny – Mike Wilner. The constant change in Watford manager, a once fine club whose first two managers lasted a total of 23 years, is now so high that I don’t even notice it anymore ... apparently this was yesterday, and I’ve no idea who the previous bloke was. Watford are now onto their 30th manager, including caretakers, although in practice they’re all just caretaker managers, since the Pozzos took over in 2012. I don’t know whether to laugh at, or cry for, the Watford fans (Narrator: it’s the former, obviously) – Noble Francis. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

articles.content: Manchester Collective, Lakeside Arts, Nottingham This take on Luke Mombrea’s Novello-winning work about a fire that burned for two months in Santa Fe, had little need of its billowing video backdrop Premieres are all well and good, but what about second performances, and third and fourth? We puzzle over the problem of new music, of how to build a living classical repertoire, while too often giving new works just one outing to make their case, audiences just one chance to hear them. How brilliant, then, to see American composer Luke Mombrea’s Black Gold – winner of a 2025 Ivor Novello award – at the centre of the Manchester Collective’s new tour: another chance to get our ears around this widescreen soundscape with its slippery electro-acoustic vistas. The fire that raged through the Santa Fe oil fields in 1928 burned for two months, swallowing up the surrounding desert in smoke and ash. Steel plate photographs show derricks dwarfed by pillars of flame and black billowing clouds. They’re the starting point for Mombrea’s chamber work, whose three movements for flute, cello, double bass and percussion were conceived in tandem with Nate Mohler’s monochrome, photo-manipulating video projections. Continue reading...

articles.content: The author blends teen memories and biographical details for a very personal tribute to the late singer When Sathnam Sanghera was a child, his older sisters fell under the spell of Wham!, the pop duo behind hits including Last Christmas and Young Guns (Go for It). Their brother soon caught the bug, becoming a diehard Wham! fan and following the career of singer George Michael into adulthood. In Tonight the Music Seems So Loud, Sanghera blends memoir, biography and cultural criticism as he explores the life and work of Michael via themed chapters covering the singer’s sexuality, activism, addictions, his Greek Cypriot heritage and his songwriting prowess. This is no objective trawl through the life of a distant pop star. Immersing himself in Michael’s world, Sanghera rides the same London bus route that he was on when he wrote Careless Whisper at 17 and visits the restaurant that once belonged to his father (Michael worked there briefly, until his dad fired him for mixing up the drinks orders). Continue reading...

articles.author: As told to Magnus Nome
articles.content: As the Norwegian pop trio’s frontman releases his new album Human Grace, he answers your questions on the devastating effects of fame, living in squalor in London, 80s nostalgia – and a certain bandmate’s denim underwear You ’ ve described your new album, Human Grace, as revealing more of yourself than your previous work. Was there anything you found unexpectedly difficult to express through these songs, or anything that surprised you about yourself during the creative process? BarefootJax No. It’s an exploratory process, the activity of making new music. It’s about quieting yourself, being available to hear tiny little differences in vibes, to pick up a seed that will blossom into something – and then it goes from being nothing to becoming a thing, instantaneously. That has never changed for me. With a-ha, there wasn’t much time and peace for songwriting. Being the frontman takes a lot of focus. What has changed is my access to the skilled tools – singing and guitar – due to the Parkinson’s medication side-effects. For this album, we found old recordings of my voice, some from over 10 years back. It hasn’t been devastating for me to get this diagnosis – it has been a blunt and impactful instrument to stop everything I was doing. I had to reassemble myself first, to understand what it is. Losing access to parts of myself I’ve taken for granted all my life, but also a new appreciation for the architecture of ourselves as an organism – it’s so impressive. It’s mind-blowing. Continue reading...

articles.content: Approval would be celebrated by the oil giants, but it wouldn’t help our constituents who worry about the climate crisis, and their bills Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire Labour split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs This week it was confirmed that millions of households are facing yet another winter of unaffordable energy bills , just as we learn that this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths in the UK . The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. articles.content: Goodwood Art Foundation The Icelandic artist’s enigmatic monuments, melancholic landscape paintings and never-ending love song are witty, moving and ravishingly conceptual Live in the gallery a man in a dark suit and white shoes leans cabaret-style against a piano and sings about his one great love. “Jenny kissed me,” he intones in a voice both melodic and casually conversational. He croons the words of this love song again, and again, and again. Icelandic artist Ragnar Kjartansson’s durational performance (which means it takes a heck of a long time) is beguiling and beautiful. It’s also a brilliant interpretation of a small masterpiece of English Romantic poetry, Jenny Kiss’d Me, by Leigh Hunt : “Jenny kissed me when we met / Jumping from the chair she sat in.” The poet demands that “Time, you thief” write this down so that he can keep this memory of a perfect moment of love. Continue reading...

articles.content: We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford. If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people. The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers Continue reading...

articles.author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
articles.content: You don’t have to have sex because it’s ‘what’s expected’, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. But you may want to be explicit about what you do want Read more Leading questions How do I navigate being single when I’m not interested in sex with near strangers? I don’t judge anyone, consenting adults can do whatever they like – but for me, sex has to come with trust and, frankly, love, or at least the potential of love. I’m recently single after a long and toxic relationship, and I’ve never dated – I got on the dating scene and found that if I don’t try to get in someone’s pants by the third date, no matter how much of a nice time we’re having, they disappear – and in fact I’ve had some women do the old “call yourself a man” at me, in one memorable case, after they specifically said “not tonight” and I said “no problem” (the response was a frustrated “don’t you have needs?!”). I’ve tried to go along with it and do what’s expected but I don’t enjoy it, it just feels a bit wrong, and when I’ve done this it kills the vibe we had, probably because I can’t get into it properly. I’ve always been into the person, not just the body, but it takes time to get to know someone enough to feel comfortable being intimate. So how can I keep a nice relationship going, so that I can develop the trust I need for sex, without them losing interest because I’m not doing (what I assume) everyone else on the dating scene is doing? Continue reading...

articles.content: Laura van der Heijden/Jâms Coleman (Chandos) The piano-cello duo explore the consoling beauty of works by Franck, Fauré and Mel Bonis, with a welcome rediscovery among the highlights This is the third release from the team of cellist Laura van der Heijden and pianist Jâms Coleman . They say it grew from a desire to record “music of consolation and warmth”, and every piece on this all-French programme fits the bill. The most substantial is Franck’s 1886 Sonata, best known in its original, violin-and-piano version but also claimed by cellists ever since the composer sanctioned an arrangement not long after its premiere. It gets a persuasively expansive performance here. Coleman’s piano is unfailingly clear and detailed; van der Heijden’s playing is angry and urgent in the second movement, impassioned in the climactic passages of the finale. More generally, though, her melodies spool out in endless lines, her tone rich and sustained, her phrasing unbroken almost to a fault: just occasionally the cello line feels as if it could use more breath, more space in which to ask questions. There’s a sense of security in that sustained tone, though, and it serves the consolatory aspect of the programme well. Massenet’s Méditation from Thaïs and Fauré’s bittersweet Sicilienne are the most familiar of the shorter pieces; alongside these there are a transcription of Paix, a melancholy yet consolatory song by Charlotte Sohy; the compact and characterful Three Pieces by Nadia Boulanger; and a characteristically lovely Élégie by the still-underrated Darius Milhaud. And from Franck’s protege Mel Bonis we hear the 1904 Cello Sonata, a searching work that manages to feel tautly argued and rhapsodic at the same time – a worthwhile rediscovery. Continue reading...

articles.author: Rachel Roddy
articles.content: ​I set out to visit the supermarket in Vatican City and discovered who can actually shop there and what they might be cooking A couple of years ago, it was announced that the supermarket inside Vatican City was to be taken over by the Gabrielli group and become one of their medium-sized Tigre stores “known for daily freshness and a welcoming and courteous atmosphere”. I remember reading this announcement in Roma Today and assuming the new supermarket would be like the impeccably efficient Vatican post office and open to everyone, and that one day I would share a freezer aisle with cardinals, nuns and off-duty Swiss Guards. Fast forward two years to the Feast team’s discovery that Vatican City is one of two countries in which there are no Feast app users (the other is North Korea). “What do they eat in Vatican City?” was the next question. Bingo, I thought, knowing exactly where Vatican residents do at least some of their shopping. Here was my chance to shop and to investigate, and to see if the special offers at our local Tigre are the same as in Papa Leo XIV’s hood in Vatican City, the smallest independent state in the world. Continue reading...

articles.content: Having built its reputation on big, brash reds, the centre of US winemaking is keeping pace with changing tastes and now becoming known for crisp whites, too I was always more of a Dawson’s Creek girlie than a fan of The OC , yet the subject of this column has found me wrestling with the earworm that is the latter’s theme tune : “California, here we come/Right back where we started from.” For Scribe Winery , at the southern end of the Sonoma Valley, this is apt, though I’m not sure winemaker Andrew Mariani would thank me for the comparison. Since buying 100 hectares here in 2007, he and his brother, Adam, have been restoring the land to viticulture after an interlude as a turkey farm. Some of the Marianis’ vines are riesling and sylvaner, honouring the German immigrant family who first cultivated them here in the 1850s, but they make up a small proportion of Scribe’s production, which is focused on bright, bracing chardonnay and terroir-driven pinot noir. It’s an approach that reflects the trend of drinkers turning away from the beefy reds, particularly cabernet sauvignon, that made California famous, towards fresher – dare I say Old World? – styles. Andrew has pulled up “cab” on recently acquired land to make room for more pinot, and his chardonnays see no oak, which has long been associated with California whites. Some even go into keg, making them more accessible. Continue reading...

articles.author: Tariq Goddard
articles.content: Bournemouth International Centre Kicking off yet another UK leg of his Never Ending Tour, Dylan may seem to treat his audience with indifference – but his songs are given imaginative, probing arrangements Norman Mailer once asked whether a reader would finish The Old Man and the Sea if they did not already know Ernest Hemingway was the author. There are moments during this Bob Dylan set – the first of another UK leg of his so-called Never Ending Tour – where I wonder what we would make of tonight’s music if we were not aware of the identity of the now 85-year-old performer. Ever since beginning the Never Ending Tour in the late 80s, Dylan has disdained crowd pleasing platitudes, preferring to reinterpret his vast oeuvre in his inimitable “late style”: the subdued jazz version of Tangled Up in Blue dropped halfway through the show is typical of his tendency to insulate old material in a new arrangement. Dylan’s decision to kick off these dates in Bournemouth at a time of year when the town’s wealthy snowbirds will have headed farther south, exhibits the same wilfulness, as does the very way he performs on stage. One can imagine Dylan rattling through tonight’s set even if the BIC were empty, a scenario completely congruous with his apparent indifference to the audience hellbent on deciphering his every syllable. Continue reading...

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.content: PC; Cosy Lives/Free Lives Catering to the exacting whims of a small town preparing for some grand visitors presents absorbing, beautifully designed – and surprisingly thrilling – challenges The small town of Twillford is abuzz with intrigue and excitement. A local duke has died and ladies of a certain standing are determined to make an impression at the funeral. As a newly arrived dressmaker with the only clothing shop in the area, you’re about to get plenty of work. Thus begins this utterly delightful sim game, in which you talk to customers, gather their style preferences and tailor specific outfits just for them. It could be a suitably respectful funeral frock, with just a hint of style to catch the eye of the duke’s wealthy relatives, or perhaps a work outfit for a farmer who loves bright colours. Once you have your brief, you open your sketchbook and draft a pattern using fabric swatches and a pencil to colour in your design. Need something elegant? How about a strapless bodice. articles.content: ( Mashwrks) Sharp, unsentimental rhymes and a fearless disregard for genre make Scenes a richly varied victory lap for for one of grime’s most distinctive talents It’s not often that a UK rap album arrives accompanied by its own air freshener and video game, but here we are. Head over to Novelist’s website, and you can find not merely the usual means of promoting a new release – branded hoodies, T-shirts and so on – but a scented mirror hanger that bears the album’s artwork and Scenes: the Drive, a vaguely Mario Kart-ish arcade game that involves driving around the landmarks of London and Los Angeles avoiding buses and the attentions of the traffic police to the strains of an album track called Prime. But then, from the moment he appeared on the grime scene in his teens – so young he now constitutes an elder statesman in his late 20s – the south Londoner has cut something of a maverick figure in the world of UK rap. He arrived bearing a moniker that seemed oddly bookish among his more grittily named peers. His early releases saw him working alongside defiantly left-field producer Mumdance. He attracted a lot of press attention of the “grime’s brightest new hope” variety, but seemed to last about 20 minutes on the high-profile XL label before departing to start his own imprint, Mmmyeh. Continue reading...

articles.content: Bottom sides could face top Nations Cup sides from 2030 Tier-one teams expected to push back against plans Two teams could be relegated from the Nations Championship from 2030 under controversial plans being developed by the tournament organisers. articles.author: Frédéric Noy
articles.content: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa. Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods. A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy Continue reading...

articles.author: Emine Saner
articles.content: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too. The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.” We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!” Continue reading...

articles.author: Devi Sridhar
articles.content: Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries . By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes , driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

articles.author: Kat Lister
articles.content: The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law “Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs. Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”. Continue reading...

articles.author: Eloise Cooke
articles.content: A new exhibition celebrates landmark artists who sliced up existing works to make striking new pieces. The show’s curators discuss how, in order to create, sometimes you first need to destroy When Valerie Solanas sold her SCUM Manifesto in 1967 it was priced at 10 cents for women and $1 for men. Artist Justine Kurland considered doing something similar with her “man books”: sell them off cheap to undermine their cultural weight. But knowing that people would just flip the books for a profit, instead she took a knife to what she calls the “problem of language and history and inheritance” in photography. She went through her own library of canonical male photographers, cut up the books and made collages from the spoils. Kurland called the project SCUMB (Society for Cutting Up Men’s Books), after Solanas’s manifesto. The same idea underpins What Rose from the Cut, a group show at Graces Mews Gallery in south London. Co-curated by Kurland, the V&A Parasol Foundation curator of women in photography Fiona Rogers, and collector Sarah Miller Meigs, the show brings together more than 40 artists working in collage, photomontage and assemblage, across three generations. All the artists share a simple aim: to make something new out of something already there. The result is no one thing: the show is erotic, sentimental, irreverent and sobering, often all at once. “There is something very specific to the idea of what it is to tear something apart,” Kurland says. “There are so many things that collage immediately does right out the door.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Ed Aarons
articles.content: Crystal Palace’s influential supporters’ group disbanded 24 hours before their first home game this season – and Selhurst Park has not been the same since Simon Teesdale could not help feeling mixed emotions when his beloved Crystal Palace won the Conference League in Leipzig in May. He started going to Selhurst Park with his father in the 1980s, became a season-ticket holder in the 1990s and has watched with pride as the club established itself as a permanent fixture in the Premier League over the past 14 years. Palace finally secured a major trophy in the 2025 FA Cup final – an experience Teesdale remembers as “one of the best days of my life” – and followed that up by winning the Conference League but he decided in August not to renew his season ticket. “Something happened between the FA Cup win and today that changed me,” he wrote in an emotional article published last month on his website. “Tipped me over the edge. Actually, it’s fairer to say that something accelerated in that period of time. The seeds were sown years ago.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Daniel Dylan Wray
articles.content: Backed by the KLF, a monument is being built using 34,592 bricks, each containing a deceased person’s glazed ashes. Is this the future of funerals? We join emotional marchers on Birkenhead’s smoky, noisy Day of the Dead Hundreds of people wearing hi-vis clothing are on a death march through Birkenhead Park. A burning shopping trolley leads the way, smoke grenades clog the air, and people holding traffic signs chant: “The dead don’t stop – till they reach the top.” There’s a wave of curtain-twitching from residents who look on with fear and bemusement as what looks like a psychedelic building site gone rogue marches through their beautiful recreation space. Where could they be going? The answer might shock some of them. For this crowd are on their way to build a pyramid … made of dead people. “My brother calls it my ‘anarchist death cult,’” laughs Steve Lowe, chief engineer of L-13 Light Industrial Workshop, who is involved in running Birkenhead Day of the Dead and the People’s Pyramid. It’s an event that has taken place every year (except 2020) since 2018 in a variety of locations and was announced by Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond of the KLF (AKA the Justified Ancients of Mu Mu AKA K2 Plant Hire Ltd), the seminal electronic duo and experimental art provocateurs, when they returned after 23 years in 2017. Continue reading...

articles.author: Chris Wiegand
articles.content: A wave of shows, including High School Musical and Rent, are upping the drama by placing viewers alongside actors. What are the risks and rewards? In the socially distanced summer of 2020, Jesus Christ Superstar was staged at Regent’s Park in London for a hugely pruned audience. Like the actors, we were kept two metres apart. It was a triumphant but extremely strange experience – not least from my current perspective. I’m standing on stage at Theatre Royal Drury Lane, jostling alongside other theatregoers, watching a miraculous revival of the same production. But this time, 75 audience members have been given a spot within the scaffold-style set for the show, beneath the musicians and almost side by side with the cast. We feel the energy of the ensemble’s dance moves, seem to join the crowd of Jesus’s followers – and those who conspire against him – and come extraordinarily close to the musical’s star, Sam Ryder, who rests right by my feet after his solo Gethsemane. It’s as close as I’ve been to the beating heart of a big West End production. Until, that is, the following week when I watch the captivating revival of Rent at the Tom Stoppard theatre from one of 82 audience seats arranged in a semicircle on stage. (Mine is just beneath a shelf bearing candle-filled wine bottles – a marker of La Vie Bohème.) Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo bounds past on to the stage, the actors mingle with us and the band are only just out of reach. Continue reading...

articles.author: Rebecca Wait
articles.content: The beautiful and mercenary Honey is a monstrously compelling character, in a novel with the ruthlessness of Richard Yates but more wit ‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury inner circle and then (in her own view, at least) just as quickly dropped again. Jenkins soon regretted the novel’s publication, apparently afraid acquaintances might recognise themselves, and tried to get rid of as many copies as she could. Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jon Bryant
articles.content: Market stalls are laden with local delicacies in the run-up to Christmas, while the city’s elegant cafes make the perfect spot to sit and watch the world go by Famous for its fabulous fruit and vegetable markets, Aix-en-Provence extends its stalls in winter to include les treize desserts de Noël , the 13 desserts of a traditional Provençal Christmas. I buy almonds (which represent the Carmelites), dried figs (Franciscans), walnuts (Augustinians) and raisins (Dominicans) from the Place Richelme market. Then I queue up in the Place des Prêcheurs for oreillettes (sweet, ear-shaped wafers), gingerbread, and white and black nougat (representing good and evil). Calissons d’Aix, the city’s celebrated, lozenge-shaped sweets, come from the smart Brémond or Le Roy René confiseries nearby. These desserts are laid out on tables in Provençal homes for the Christmas period interspersed with santons (tiny clay figurines), which are sold at Aix’s Foire aux Santons from mid-November. articles.author: Zoe Williams
articles.content: Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world. Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously , from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers ? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference. articles.author: Rachel Roddy
articles.content: Soft, plump, sweet-savoury rolls marry historical English breakfast baps with a culinary tradition from Italy’s mountainous Trentino-Südtirol In Elizabeth David’s English Bread and Yeast Cookery , there’s a chapter called “Manchets, Mayn and Payndemayn”, all of which were 15th-century names for rarefied soft white bread made from the finest wheat flour. As well as pages of historical context that only she could make so lively, David includes a 1615 recipe for manchet from a book called The English Huswife that calls for meal to be ground into the whitest flower, mixed with ale yeast, salt and liquor (a mixture of water and milk), before being wrapped in a cloth, kneaded with feet, left to swell, shaped, then baked in a gentle heat. It is this form of manchet that David sees as being the common ancestor of all English breakfast breads: baps, soft rolls and dough cakes, with the presence of milk (and, therefore, fat) ensuring both crumb and crust are soft. In fact, her recipe for breakfast baps (or, rather, a recipe from Mr CG Lockyer from Crewkerne) is almost identical to manchet, although without the millstones, dough tub and feet. Continue reading...

articles.author: Mona Chalabi
articles.content: I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18. Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. Because my parents were immigrants, they had no family in Britain – no one they could ask to watch us for a couple of hours without payment, let alone look out for us after they were gone. So, just before I started secondary school, my mum asked one of my friends’ parents if she could name them as our next of kin. They said yes, but not wanting to rely on others, she continued to work hard to ensure we, as well as her family in Iraq, would have as much financial security as possible. Continue reading...

articles.content: Photographer David Levene meets service personnel and veterans at selection trials in Lviv for next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham It took a little longer than expected for the 100 or so archers to begin competing inside the large Soviet-era velodrome arena at MoD SKA in Lviv (built for the 1980 Moscow Olympics, it is Ukraine’s only indoor cycling track) on the first day of trials for the team that Ukraine will send to next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham . articles.author: Kirsty Major
articles.content: Luyen Vu’s discount eye surgeries represent the dangers of an unregulated beauty industry. But for her fans, she is a folk hero Robert Laycock, a facial plastic surgeon at Aintree University Hospital in Liverpool, first knew that something was up when a patient came to him in early 2024. She was a woman in her 40s who had undergone a blepharoplasty, a procedure that involves making an incision just below or above the eyelids and removing small amounts of skin and sometimes fat and muscle. The point of the surgery is to make the patient’s face look more youthful. This woman’s stitches, however, had started coming apart, leaving an open wound right above her eyes. It is not unusual for botched private cosmetic surgeries to be fixed on the NHS. Laycock estimates that he sees three or four patients a year who need surgical intervention after too much tissue has been removed in a blepharoplasty. But something was different about this woman. “The surgery was done in a very odd way,” Laycock told me. The incision, he explained, had been made just beneath the eyebrow rather than on the crease of the eyelid. “[It’s] not the way that we would generally do a blepharoplasty in the UK.” He asked the woman where she’d had the work done but she was evasive and he dropped the subject. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alex Needham
articles.content: He’s been pierced, chained, inflated, stretched, suctioned and denounced in the Senate. As Ron Athey hits the UK, he talks about his upbringing in ‘a cult’ – and why being naked just isn’t enough ‘The nicest way to say what I do is that I want to create a miracle,” says Ron Athey. “The gnarly way is that I know what the edges are when it comes to the mortification of the flesh.” The softly spoken performance art legend has come to the Guardian’s offices in a flat cap and navy blue Fred Perry hoodie. Only his facial tattoos and platform boots hint at the fact that he has been responsible for some of the most extreme works of live art of all time. Take Self-Obliteration, which begins with a naked Athey violently brushing a long blond wig pinned to his head with blunt needles, before tearing it off, upon which blood pours down his face and on to his body. (Blunt needles, you see, make bigger holes.) Or Solar Anus, in which he puts hooks in his face that stretch the skin of his cheeks and eyes, turning his face into a kind of ancient Egyptian death mask. In St Sebastian, Athey is suspended by chains while assistants pierce his flesh with arrows and needles. Continue reading...

articles.author: Hannah J Davies
articles.content: The star was chewed up and spewed out by the tabloids after the Sun on Sunday sting in 2013. But she is disarming in this fight for change – and ready to ‘raise a bit of hell’ In 2011, Tulisa Contostavlos was at the peak of her powers. At 22, the N-Dubz singer turned solo artist had landed a coveted position as a judge on The X Factor, stepping into Cheryl Cole’s towering stilettos. As she puts it here, her pitch to X Factor supremo Simon Cowell was simple: “You’re gonna need someone to sit there and look pretty and cry when [there are] emotional moments, and you’re gonna need someone to tell people they’re rubbish when they’re rubbish – and I’m gonna do both.” Cowell hired her on the spot, she says. Tulisa was a household name, but sections of the British media treated her with contempt, with headlines that played up her working-class background and labelled her a chav. Much of this three-part series is concentrated, however, on the most egregious example of the press turning on her: a sting by the Sun on Sunday in 2013, which saw Tulisa groomed into believing she was auditioning for a Hollywood film over the course of several months. Eventually, she was asked to supply drugs to a producer, and – under pressure to please her new bosses – passed a phone number to the infamous Sun journalist Mazher Mahmood, AKA The Fake Sheikh. But she is disarming in this fight for change – and ready to ‘raise a bit of hell’ In 2011, Tulisa Contostavlos was at the peak of her powers. At 22, the N-Dubz singer turned solo artist had landed a coveted position as a judge on The X Factor, stepping into Cheryl Cole’s towering stilettos. As she puts it here, her pitch to X Factor supremo Simon Cowell was simple: “You’re gonna need someone to sit there and look pretty and cry when [there are] emotional moments, and you’re gonna need someone to tell people they’re rubbish when they’re rubbish – and I’m gonna do both.” Cowell hired her on the spot, she says. Tulisa was a household name, but sections of the British media treated her with contempt, with headlines that played up her working-class background and labelled her a chav. Much of this three-part series is concentrated, however, on the most egregious example of the press turning on her: a sting by the Sun on Sunday in 2013, which saw Tulisa groomed into believing she was auditioning for a Hollywood film over the course of several months. Eventually, she was asked to supply drugs to a producer, and – under pressure to please her new bosses – passed a phone number to the infamous Sun journalist Mazher Mahmood, AKA The Fake Sheikh. Continue reading...
articles.title: Tulisa: The Reckoning review – it’s hard to believe how far the disgusting drugs set-up went

articles.content: Federal judge Loren L AliKhan grants preliminary injunction in ABC’s favor after network sued FCC in August The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network sued the agency in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns. The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel. Continue reading...

articles.content: The guitarist was absolutely integral to Duran Duran’s success, and not merely because he was by far the band’s most straightforwardly talented musician Andy Taylor, guitarist in Duran Duran, dies aged 65 Andy Taylor – a life in pictures It’s very easy indeed to paint Andy Taylor as the misfit within the world-beating five-man line-up of Duran Duran. The others were fans of glam and Chic: their avowed intention was to form a band that melded the sophisticated disco of the latter with the extravagant style and experimental art-pop of Roxy Music. Taylor – who had made what he later called “that fateful journey down to Birmingham” from his home on Tyneside after spotting an ad in the Melody Maker – had tastes that tended towards rock music of a more traditional stripe, as evidenced by the artists he covered on his second solo album, 1990’s Dangerous: Thin Lizzy, Bad Company, AC/DC, Montrose. Continue reading...

articles.content: From a half-time huddle gone wrong to an ultimatum over play-calling, here’s what the quarterback said Wednesday in a scorched-earth appearance on Pat McAfee’s show Barely 12 hours after the Pittsburgh Steelers announced that Aaron Rodgers would be deactivated and Mason Rudolph would start Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos, the four-time NFL Most Valuable Player left no bridge unburned in a surprise call-in to ESPN’s The Pat McAfee Show. In a 34-minute appearance on Wednesday afternoon where he spoke uninterrupted for long stretches, Rodgers accused Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy of falling asleep in a quarterback meeting, skipping walkthroughs and falling behind on film study. He also said the 63-year-old McCarthy broke a half-time huddle against Philadelphia with the words “One, two, three, Packers”. According to Rodgers, McCarthy denied falling asleep at the team facility. Continue reading...

articles.content: Wired, wireless, noise cancelling and budget … here are the headphones to level up your PC and console gaming • The best gaming chairs We talk a lot about graphics in video games; we know how important it is to play on a decent screen so we can see what we’re shooting at … or running away from. But what about sound? Explosions, dialogue, the wheezy breathing of a nearby monster – arguably, audio quality is just as important. Many modern games now support 3D or spatial audio, which lets you detect exactly where a sound is coming from in the game world. In survival horror adventures, you can hear the zombie lurking in the next room, and in popular shooters such as Fortnite and Apex Legends, you can pinpoint the footsteps of approaching enemies. Continue reading...

articles.content: Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’ Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”. This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem. articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends. Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight . With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time. articles.content: It feels as if we’re destined to hold the same referendum every decade. Nige, Arron and co are up for the fight Roll back the years. The Bad Boys of Brexit have reformed and are back in town. Andy Wigmore on comms. Arron Banks on lead vocals and money. Nigel Farage on doing whatever the hell he likes. Apart from spending his own cash on security. This time round, though, a woman has joined the band. Step forward, Catherine McBride. Probably the only woman alive who Nige thinks he can trust not to be totally pissed by 3pm. Even so, you can sense that this is a relationship destined to end in tears. Give it a couple of months and Catherine will be wishing she had never met Nige and Arron. Continue reading...

articles.content: Controlled blast to dispose of lead azide risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in 100-mile radius The US army detonated the nation’s entire stockpile of the the bomb-making material lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. The controlled blast, which took place at about 10.00am ET, was to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the chemical that was stored at the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people. articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.content: Readers on the failure of the climate talks in Turkey and the lessons we can learn The failure of Cop31, as commented on by Bill McGuire ( A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November ), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption. The disjunction between peril and necessary action is explained by the impossibility of taming appetites that are insatiable. It is convenient to blame fossil fuel producers, and while they are obviously guilty parties, the ultimate problem is the continuing demand for their products. Continue reading...

articles.content: Raymond T Pierrehumbert and Dr Lynne Jones respond to an article by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh Watching Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, forced to defend the government’s retreat from net zero ( Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep, 17 November ) was painfully reminiscent of the way in which Colin Powell, a former US secretary of state and an honourable man, was forced to defend George W Bush’s claims justifying the disastrous Iraq war. Fahnbulleh states that people need to see the benefits of net zero on their doorstep – meaning jobs, cost of living and warm homes. But in fact the policies of this government mark a retreat of all of these “doorstep” benefits. Andy Burnham has slashed heat pump subsidies , which means more vulnerability of homes to heating price shocks from international affairs spiking fossil gas prices; it also means fewer warm homes and jobs in the heat pump manufacturing and installation industry. Continue reading...

articles.content: To distort what was actually a reduction in supply into a reduction in demand and then use it as ‘evidence’ is unworthy of our world-class research institution, says Marcia Saunders After a cyber-attack in 2023 , which Ciaran Martin, a former CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre, described as “ one of the worst cyber incidents in British history ”, use of the British Library’s reading rooms fell dramatically ( British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces, 20 November ). Throughout 2024-25, services were heavily affected, including archives, manuscripts, books and online journal articles. All readers’ tickets were suspended and initially were reissued for limited periods of time. It should surprise no one that use of the reading rooms fell off. Only last month was access to the UK web archive (partially) restored. Continue reading...

articles.content: Omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that ‘magisterial’ civic amenities just happen by magic, writes Beth Breeze . Plus letters from Rendel Harris and Tom Uprichard Oliver Wainwright’s extremely positive review of the “magisterial” new London Museum will encourage many to visit ( Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight, 24 November ). But amid the praise for the architects who masterminded this transformation, and the well‑aimed barbs at the City of London Corporation, which tried to prevent it, there is no mention of those who provided the all-important funding. In particular, omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that fantastic civic amenities just happen by magic, or are totally funded by taxpayers. articles.content: Measles is spreading across the world and could give rise to another pandemic, writes Colette McIvor After reading your report ( ‘They’re struggling for oxygen’: children pay the price as countries allow measles to surge again, 20 November ), I was struck by the statement that proposed cuts to foreign aid from wealthy countries are likely to exacerbate the problem, particularly for those within developing countries. The UK intends to cut foreign aid spending from 0.5% to 0.3% of national income by the end of 2027. Worryingly, in its 2025-26 report, the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office proposed a cut of 35% on funding provided to the Democratic Republic of Congo . As your article pointed out, the DRC is already experiencing a deadly Ebola outbreak; with the spread of measles, thousands more will be lost to a different, and largely preventable disease. Continue reading...

articles.content: (Atlantic) Justice bring some 80s nostalgia but this compilation of new material from music’s A-list – from Dua Lipa to Travis Scott and a host of Latin talent – stays at the cutting edge It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish. Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. This style is synonymous with Grand Theft Auto VI’s setting, a fictionalised version of Florida last seen in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was beloved for its inclusion of 80s hits. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ben Eastham
articles.content: White Cube Bermondsey, London Kiefer asks what art means after the Holocaust – but even the vast scale of his powerfully seductive paintings can’t do justice to the gravity of his themes When the world is falling apart, the artist retreats to the studio. It’s an old story, and Anselm Kiefer has always loved the old stories, drawing for his monumental and reliably blockbuster paintings on narrative traditions ranging from Norse mythology to German Romantic poetry. So it makes sense that an artist who has dedicated his life to the question of what art means after the end of European civilisation – which is to say, after the Holocaust – should now seek out the solitude of the studio to make sense of what’s coming. Kiefer’s exhibition at the same gallery a decade ago had the title Walhalla , after the beer hall in the sky in which dead Vikings drink away the afterlife. Now comes the more modest (you would think) subject of the artist’s studio, depicted here in a suite of lustrous landscapes and a simple wooden cabin in the forest. Rendered in flat gold leaf, the sky in these paintings gleams like a tarnished halo in an old altarpiece, while the verdigris grass pushes roughly off the canvas. Here is the place where heaven meets the earth and is transmuted – by the alchemy of this painter’s touch – into quietly numinous paintings containing elements of both. If you can put aside the fact that Kiefer’s own studio is a vast warehouse complex on the outskirts of Paris, these paintings present a very German vision of communion with nature. They also evoke the most famous hut in modern philosophy: the Black Forest hideaway where Martin Heidegger formulated his argument that “authentic” culture must be rooted in the native landscape. The flipside of this idea, that nature is not just a scenic backdrop to human history but a living participant in it, would have, let’s just say, consequences for German painting after 1945. Here is the challenge that Kiefer has spent his career meeting: how to paint the landscape as an unspoilt refuge from society when it is littered with mass graves? Continue reading...

articles.author: Ben Fisher in Istanbul
articles.content: Unai Emery wanted the winger but, like Harvey Elliott last season, he has been left out in the cold despite Villa’s attacking struggles It is three years this week since Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring for Manchester United in a 3-3 draw at Galatasaray in the Champions League, on a typically boisterous night in Istanbul when Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, now his teammates at Aston Villa, were also among the starters. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award. He went on to score twice at Old Trafford on Boxing Day, in a 3-2 victory against Villa, and a couple of months later his double at home to West Ham was the catalyst for that iconic celebration photo of Garnacho, Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund sitting on the advertising hoardings at the Stretford End, beaming smiles all round. All three were at the heart of United’s plans for a bright future, beacons of hope. At the end of that season, Garnacho signed off in style, he and Mainoo scoring against Manchester City at Wembley to win the FA Cup . Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.content: Pair clashed at PMQs over a video shot outside No 10 by TikToker Max Balegde Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration. Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov. Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters. It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity. Continue reading...

articles.author: Emma Brockes
articles.content: For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape. To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett , was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”. Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.author: Nesrine Malik, in East Jerusalem
articles.content: Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure. There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem. Continue reading...

articles.content: Life100 features the wisdom of two women in their 80s and has gone viral by exploring important life lessons It is, unfortunately, a familiar scene. At the dinner table, a woman berates her granddaughter with invasive, personal questions – why are you still single? When are you going to have kids? – punctuated by unnerving thrusts of her steak knife. The granddaughter is clearly uncomfortable, but her grandmother pays no attention. Anyone who has been in this situation likely knows what comes next. The granddaughter may try to deflect, only to invite further questioning, or call out her grandmother’s rudeness, which risks escalation. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Early in the second half of Tuesday night’s National League South match between Torquay United and Chesham, play was briefly suspended due to an ear-splitting din emitted over the Plainmoor public address system. “The game has stopped because the Torquay Tannoy system is making a loud noise that won’t stop,” posted Chesham on their Social Media Disgrace account. “I’m not kidding.” A sort of aural cross between an ocean liner’s foghorn and a party conference speech delivered by a senior member of the Reform party, it eventually stopped and play resumed with Torquay running out 2-1 winners. Given the precedent of awarding/revoking/re-awarding of the Afcon 2025 edition this would be entirely justified” – Peter Martin. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. articles.author: Brian Logan
articles.content: SEC Armadillo, Glasgow The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist. The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing , and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life. Touring Europe until 2 May Continue reading...

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.content: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. Continue reading...

articles.content: Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak , which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating . Continue reading...

articles.content: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull , Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal ) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford . This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

articles.content: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. Continue reading...

articles.content: Dario Russo’s debut feature is Brothers Grimm meets Yorgos Lanthimos, with a standout cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill and Emily Browning The vibe of writer-director Dario Russo’s delightfully peculiar feature debut is “messed-up fairytale”, pitched somewhere between the Brothers Grimm and Yorgos Lanthimos, with a distinctly Australian je ne sais quoi . Russo is perhaps best known for co-creating the spy comedy series Danger 5, which had an aesthetic inspired by 60s and 70s men’s magazines; The Fox has a similarly thick retro texture. I love how this film feels as though it was made in consultation with the animal world, taking place in a universe where animals can speak to humans – though that’s perhaps the least weird thing about it. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jess Cartner-Morley
articles.content: From a V-neck sweater worn back-to-front to a perfectly framed collarbone – here’s the secret to low-stakes sex appeal I’m not sure when it started being not chic to want to look sexy, but it’s definitely a thing and it bothers me as it doesn’t feel truthful to the human experience, if that’s not a lot for the first sentence of a fashion column. Our wardrobes have become shrines to good taste. Well-cut coats and quality knitwear, elegant flat shoes and crisp white shirts. These clothes are excellent at communicating that you have read the briefing notes for the meeting and have some Booker prize chat. They are less good at suggesting you might be up for dancing on a table later. Why do we have to choose? Clothes have always been partly about how they make us feel physically. We accept that an outfit can make you feel powerful, cool, smart. Why shouldn’t it also make you feel hot and fun? Continue reading...
